connection_type: I'm a caregiver, partner, or close community member of someone with this experience
duration: Most of my professional life, 13 years or so
disclosure_text: I work in rural community pharmacy in an area with a very large hispanic population and a very narrow spectrum of income levels canted mostly towards the bottom third of earners. I have to deal with comments on these topics just about all the time.
micronarrative:
The connection is with the first group, because that feels like something that could actually happen on a regular basis, especially in my area. The group offering tea is just absurd; who would distribute hot tea at any rally? Additionally, it's a grocery store, there's bound to be multiple entrances that aren't blocked by protestors outside of a town hall meeting. My local community would have people on the defense of undocumented immigrants being the loud side, with those against just being the general population. They'd be completely silent, just assuming everybody is with them. I don't think anything close to this scenario would actually happen, because local government for sure wouldn't step in to help undocumented immigrants in rural America.

The ones against the undocumented immigrants likely wouldn't even really show up, just tossing around casual racist epithets to one another. Those for them would likely be shouting simple messages, and the vast majority of the population wouldn't care one way or another. Dialects aren't really a thing in rural America; it's more just a lack of annunciation.

I was at work helping a 90-year-old lady with her medications when she casually just mentioned she was having a lot of trouble with the "n-words" in the community, and how they wouldn't talk to her even if she engaged. I was taken very far aback, as I'm ambiguously brown, and this lady decided that I was the safe one to drop the n-bomb on? It made it very clear that even though we're in rural Colorado, there's some hardcore racism still running rampant, the likes of which you'd expect in the south. In and among all the normal racism against Hispanic cultures, this lady was comfortable talking to a pharmacist like that. Unbelievable.

annotations.tweet_text: Our hospitals can't keep up. At some point we have to ask who this country is actually for.
annotations.participant_label: Clearly harmful — targets a group in a way that dehumanises or incites
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale: The specific reference is to who the country is actually for being the clear dog whistle that indicates immigrants. It also has a very high likelihood of people who aren't directly immigrants but might be immigrant adjacent or naturalized citizens just lumped together. This is the kind of language used to invoke outrage, people are allowed to go in for healthcare, especially if they work in dangerous fields or with a lack of safety equipment as is what's usually seen with immigrant workers in this area

annotations.tweet_text: My grandparents came here legally and waited years. Why should anyone get to skip that line?
annotations.participant_label: Clearly harmful — targets a group in a way that dehumanises or incites
annotations.participant_target: Immigrants, refugees, or a racialised group
annotations.rationale: The core of this language is very much I got mine, so you don't get any, or something akin to pulling the ladder up behind you. It very much ignores the advances in technology that have happened in the past 80 years since their grandparents were immigrants, and it ignores the significantly more globalized society of today.

annotations.tweet_text: When you flood a labor market, wages go down. Economics doesn't care about feelings.
annotations.participant_label: Likely not harmful — critical or provocative, but the harm reading requires a stretch
annotations.rationale: This is much less obviously intended to hurt a specific group, and could be used in the broader category to target anyone that's trying to argue against efficient wage growth. In my field, about 10 years ago, it's the language they were using to talk about pharmacists. Of course you don't get a pay raise, we can replace you at any time with 15 others just like you.
